name: Pod resources: requests, limits & scheduling
objective: CKA › Workloads & Scheduling. Resource requests drive scheduling (the scheduler places a pod only where its requests fit a node's allocatable); limits cap usage; together they set the pod's QoS class. Set requests/limits on a workload, then diagnose a pod stuck Pending because its request exceeds every node.

questions.title: Set requests and limits (QoS)
questions.teach:
`resources.requests` is what the scheduler **reserves** on a node (and what it schedules against); `resources.limits` is the hard cap the kubelet enforces (CPU throttled, memory OOM-killed). Requests ≠ limits ⇒ the pod's **QoS class is `Burstable`** (equal requests==limits for every resource ⇒ `Guaranteed`; none set ⇒ `BestEffort`).

**Gotcha:** CPU is **compressible** (over-limit = throttled); memory is **not** (over-limit = OOMKilled). The scheduler only looks at **requests**, never limits.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `resources-learn`, create a Deployment `rated` (1 replica, image `nginx:1.25`) whose container `web` sets requests `cpu=100m, memory=64Mi` and limits `cpu=250m, memory=128Mi`.

Target: Deployment `rated` is ready; its container has those exact requests/limits, giving QoS class `Burstable`.
questions.hint: Put `resources: { requests: {cpu: 100m, memory: 64Mi}, limits: {cpu: 250m, memory: 128Mi} }` on the container. Check QoS with `kubectl -n resources-learn get pod -l app=rated -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.qosClass}'`.
questions.solution:
kubectl create namespace resources-learn 2>/dev/null
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: rated, namespace: resources-learn }
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: rated } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: rated } }
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: nginx:1.25
        resources:
          requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 64Mi }
          limits:   { cpu: 250m, memory: 128Mi }
YAML
kubectl -n resources-learn rollout status deploy/rated

verification.description: Deployment rated ready with requests 100m/64Mi, limits 250m/128Mi (QoS Burstable)

questions.eli5:
Think of a node like an airplane with a fixed number of seats (CPU) and a fixed amount of overhead-bin space (memory). Each pod is a passenger who books some of both.

A **request** is the seat you **reserve** when you book: "I need 100m of CPU and 64Mi of memory." The booking desk (the **scheduler**) only lets you board a plane that still has that much free — and once you've booked, that space is held for you whether you use it or not.

A **limit** is the **hard ceiling** on how much you're actually allowed to grab mid-flight: "you can stretch up to 250m CPU and 128Mi memory, no more." The flight attendant (the **kubelet**) enforces it.

Now the two resources behave very differently when you hit the ceiling:
- **CPU is stretchy** — go over your CPU limit and you're just **slowed down** (throttled), like being asked to type more slowly.
- **Memory is NOT stretchy** — go over your memory limit and you get **thrown off the plane** (OOMKilled), because you can't "give back" memory you already grabbed.

When your request and limit are different (like here, 100m vs 250m), Kubernetes files you under the **Burstable** class — "has a reservation, allowed to burst above it."

**Watch out for:**

- **The scheduler only reads *requests*, never limits.** Limits don't affect where a pod lands.
- **CPU over-limit = throttled; memory over-limit = OOMKilled.** Very different consequences.
- **QoS class is automatic:** requests == limits for *every* resource ⇒ **Guaranteed**; requests set but different (or only some set) ⇒ **Burstable**; nothing set ⇒ **BestEffort**.
- **Units matter:** `m` = millicores (`100m` = 0.1 CPU); memory uses `Mi`/`Gi` (binary), not `MB`/`GB`.
- A too-big **request** (not limit) is what strands a pod `Pending` — that's the next lesson.
questions.deepDive:
## Requests, limits & QoS — full rundown

### The one-sentence model
**`requests`** are what the scheduler **reserves** on a node and schedules against; **`limits`** are the hard caps the **kubelet** enforces at runtime. The relationship between them sets the pod's **QoS class**. The scheduler looks only at **requests**.

### requests vs limits
| | `requests` | `limits` |
|---|---|---|
| Who uses it | **scheduler** (placement) | **kubelet** (runtime cap) |
| Meaning | guaranteed/reserved minimum | maximum allowed |
| CPU over-cap | n/a | **throttled** (compressible) |
| Memory over-cap | n/a | **OOMKilled** (incompressible) |
| Omitted | scheduled as 0 (risky) | no cap (can starve neighbors) |

> CPU is **compressible** → exceeding the limit throttles the container. Memory is **incompressible** → exceeding the limit kills it (OOMKilled). The scheduler never consults limits.

### The manifest
```yaml
spec:
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: nginx:1.25
    resources:
      requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 64Mi }
      limits:   { cpu: 250m, memory: 128Mi }
```
Create via Deployment:
```bash
kubectl apply -f rated.yaml
kubectl -n resources-learn rollout status deploy/rated
```

### Units
| Resource | Units | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| CPU | cores / millicores | `1` = 1 core, `500m` = 0.5 core, `100m` = 0.1 core |
| Memory | binary (power-of-2) or decimal | `64Mi`=64×2²⁰ B, `128Mi`, `1Gi`; `M`/`G` are decimal (avoid mixing) |

CPU is measured in **millicores** (`m`). Memory uses `Ki/Mi/Gi` (binary) — prefer these; `Mi` ≠ `M`.

### QoS classes
Kubernetes assigns `status.qosClass` automatically from the requests/limits across **all** containers:

| QoS class | Condition | Eviction priority under node pressure |
|---|---|---|
| **Guaranteed** | every container has `requests == limits` for **both** CPU and memory | evicted **last** |
| **Burstable** | at least one request/limit set, but not Guaranteed | evicted **in the middle** |
| **BestEffort** | **no** requests or limits anywhere | evicted **first** |

This lab's pod (`100m/64Mi` requests, `250m/128Mi` limits) is **Burstable** because requests ≠ limits.

```bash
kubectl -n resources-learn get pod -l app=rated \
  -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.qosClass}'; echo      # Burstable
```

### How requests drive scheduling
The scheduler filters nodes where **sum of pod requests ≤ node Allocatable**, then scores the survivors. `limits` are ignored for placement. Inspect capacity:
```bash
kubectl describe node <node> | sed -n '/Allocatable/,/Allocated resources/p'
kubectl describe node <node> | sed -n '/Allocated resources/,/Events/p'   # current reservations
```

### Inspect
```bash
kubectl -n resources-learn get deploy rated \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources}'; echo
kubectl -n resources-learn describe pod -l app=rated | sed -n '/Limits/,/Environment/p'
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Scheduler reads requests only.** Setting a big limit changes nothing about placement.
- **CPU over-limit → throttled; memory over-limit → OOMKilled.** Don't set memory limits too tight.
- **QoS is derived, not declared.** To get **Guaranteed**, set `requests == limits` for CPU *and* memory on *every* container; any gap drops you to Burstable.
- **No requests at all = BestEffort**, scheduled as 0 and evicted first — usually not what you want.
- **Units:** `100m` CPU ≠ `100` CPU; `64Mi` ≠ `64M`. A stray unit error can massively over/under-request.
- A **LimitRange** in the namespace can inject defaults — your pod may end up with values you didn't type.

### Quick reference
```yaml
resources:
  requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 64Mi }
  limits:   { cpu: 250m, memory: 128Mi }   # requests != limits => Burstable
```
```bash
kubectl -n resources-learn rollout status deploy/rated
kubectl -n resources-learn get pod -l app=rated -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.qosClass}'; echo
```

questions.title: Diagnose & fix: a pod stuck Pending (request too big)
questions.teach:
A pod whose CPU/memory **request exceeds every node's allocatable** can never be placed — it sits `Pending` with a scheduler event `0/N nodes are available: Insufficient cpu`. The fix is on the workload: lower the request to something a node can satisfy.

**Gotcha:** this is a **request** problem, not limits — the scheduler rejects it before it ever runs. `kubectl describe pod` Events name the exact shortfall.
questions.prompt:
Setup created Deployment `hog` in `resources-learn` requesting `cpu: "6"` — more than any node's 4 allocatable CPUs — so its pod is `Pending`. Diagnose and fix it so `hog` runs (keep it reasonable, e.g. `cpu: 200m`).

Target: Deployment `hog` has 1 ready replica and its container's CPU request is ≤ 1 core.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n resources-learn describe pod -l app=hog` → 'Insufficient cpu'. Lower the request: `kubectl -n resources-learn patch deploy hog --type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources/requests/cpu","value":"200m"}]'` (or edit the Deployment).
questions.solution:
kubectl -n resources-learn patch deploy hog --type=json \
  -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources/requests/cpu","value":"200m"}]'
kubectl -n resources-learn rollout status deploy/hog

verification.description: Deployment hog scheduled & ready after reducing its CPU request

questions.eli5:
Back to the airplane. A pod is a passenger, and the **request** is the space they reserve when booking. The booking desk (the **scheduler**) will only seat you on a plane that has enough free space for your reservation.

Now imagine a passenger walks up and demands **6 whole rows to themselves** — but every plane in the fleet only has **4 rows total**. No plane can ever fit that booking, so the passenger just stands at the gate forever. That's a pod stuck in **`Pending`**: Deployment `hog` asked for `cpu: "6"`, but each node only has **4 allocatable CPUs**, so the scheduler can't place it anywhere.

The giveaway is in the pod's events. Run `kubectl -n resources-learn describe pod -l app=hog` and you'll see a line like **`0/N nodes are available: Insufficient cpu`** — the scheduler literally telling you nobody has room.

The fix: shrink the booking. Lower the CPU **request** to something a plane can actually fit, e.g. `200m` (a fifth of one CPU). Patch the Deployment and the scheduler immediately seats the new pod.

**Watch out for:**

- **This is a *request* problem, not a *limit* problem.** The scheduler rejects it before it ever runs; limits never affect placement.
- **`Pending` + `Insufficient cpu` in Events = request too big for any node.** Always read `kubectl describe pod` events.
- **Compare against *allocatable*, not total capacity** — the OS and system pods reserve some, so allocatable is a bit less than the raw core count.
- **Memory works the same way** (`Insufficient memory`) — the same diagnosis and fix.
- **Fix the Deployment's pod template**, then wait for the rollout; the old Pending pod is replaced by one that fits.
questions.deepDive:
## Pod stuck Pending — request too big — full rundown

### The one-sentence model
The scheduler places a pod only on a node whose **Allocatable** can satisfy the pod's **requests**. If a pod's CPU (or memory) request exceeds **every** node's allocatable, it can never be placed and sits **`Pending`** with `0/N nodes are available: Insufficient cpu`. Fix the **request** on the workload.

### Diagnosis
```bash
kubectl -n resources-learn get pods -l app=hog          # STATUS = Pending
kubectl -n resources-learn describe pod -l app=hog | sed -n '/Events/,$p'
# Warning  FailedScheduling  0/3 nodes are available:
#   3 Insufficient cpu. preemption: 0/3 nodes are available ...
```
The event names the exact resource shortfall (`Insufficient cpu` / `Insufficient memory`).

Check what nodes actually offer:
```bash
kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,CPU:.status.allocatable.cpu,MEM:.status.allocatable.memory
kubectl describe node <node> | sed -n '/Allocatable/,/Allocated resources/p'
```
`hog` requests `cpu: "6"`; each node has **4** allocatable CPUs → no fit anywhere.

### Capacity vs Allocatable
| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `status.capacity` | Total hardware on the node |
| `status.allocatable` | Capacity **minus** kube/system reserved — what the scheduler can hand out |

Always compare requests against **Allocatable**, not Capacity.

### The fix — lower the request
```bash
# JSON patch (surgical)
kubectl -n resources-learn patch deploy hog --type=json \
  -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources/requests/cpu","value":"200m"}]'
kubectl -n resources-learn rollout status deploy/hog
```
Alternatives:
```bash
kubectl -n resources-learn set resources deploy hog --requests=cpu=200m
kubectl -n resources-learn edit deploy hog        # change requests.cpu by hand
```
Editing the Deployment template creates a **new** pod that fits; the old `Pending` pod is removed by the rollout.

### Common FailedScheduling reasons (read the Events)
| Event text | Cause |
|---|---|
| `Insufficient cpu` / `Insufficient memory` | Request exceeds allocatable on every node |
| `node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector` | `nodeSelector`/affinity matches no node |
| `node(s) had untolerated taint {...}` | Missing toleration for a node taint |
| `node(s) had volume node affinity conflict` | PV is zone-locked away from candidate nodes |
| `too many pods` | Node at its max-pods limit |

Only the first row is this lab's cause, but the exam mixes them — always read the event.

### Requests vs limits (why it's requests)
The scheduler **only** evaluates `requests`. A huge `limit` with a small `request` still schedules fine; a huge `request` fails placement regardless of limits. This is strictly a **request** problem.

### Verify the fix
```bash
kubectl -n resources-learn get deploy hog
kubectl -n resources-learn get pods -l app=hog -o wide       # Running, has a NODE
kubectl -n resources-learn get deploy hog \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources.requests.cpu}'; echo   # 200m
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **It's the request, not the limit.** Lowering the limit does nothing; lower the **request**.
- **Pending with FailedScheduling** → always `describe pod` and read the reason; don't guess.
- **Allocatable < Capacity** — a request equal to raw core count can still fail due to system reservations.
- **Memory shortfalls** present identically (`Insufficient memory`) — same fix.
- **Patch the Deployment template**, not the (soon-replaced) pod; then `rollout status`.
- `requests: cpu: "6"` (quoted) = 6 **whole cores**; don't confuse with `6m`.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n resources-learn describe pod -l app=hog | sed -n '/Events/,$p'   # Insufficient cpu
kubectl -n resources-learn set resources deploy hog --requests=cpu=200m
kubectl -n resources-learn rollout status deploy/hog
```
